sections.title: Metallomic Signature
sections.html:
Metallomic Signature

The tuberculosis metallome is organized around a single contested element: iron. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) requires iron for growth and virulence, and it deploys a dedicated piracy apparatus to extract it from the host. Two siderophores do the work: cell-wall-associated mycobactin and secreted carboxymycobactin, both high-affinity Fe3+ chelators capable of stripping iron from transferrin, lactoferrin, and ferritin. Ferric-carboxymycobactin is internalized by the IrtAB transporter, whose IrtA domain reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+ during import; the entire system is governed by the iron-dependent regulator IdeR, which derepresses uptake under iron starvation. {{cite:RodriguezIron}} Genetic disruption of siderophore synthesis or uptake abolishes survival in low-iron medium and inside macrophages, confirming that this machinery is essential rather than accessory. {{cite:RodriguezIron}}{{cite:IrtAB}}

The host counters by withholding iron. In active TB, IL-6 drives hepcidin, which degrades the iron exporter ferroportin, producing hypoferremia and the functional anemia of inflammation. {{cite:HepcidinAxis}} The critical interpretive point is that low serum iron in TB is sequestration, not depletion: macrophage and tissue iron is often retained or elevated even as circulating iron falls. {{cite:HostIronStatus}} This matters because the opposite state is dangerous. Macrophage iron loading and high dietary iron worsen TB outcomes — the African dietary-iron-overload (siderosis) literature links iron loading to increased TB risk and mortality — and serum ferritin tracks disease severity. {{cite:AfricaOverload}}{{cite:HostIronStatus}}

Beyond iron, the host weaponizes copper and zinc, flooding the Mtb-containing phagosome with toxic concentrations of both metals. A burst of free zinc and intraphagosomal zinc accumulation occurs within hours of infection in human macrophages; Mtb survives by exporting it through the P-type ATPase CtpC. {{cite:Botella}} Copper intoxication is resisted through the efflux ATPase CtpV (co-regulated with the copper sensor CsoR) and the outer-membrane channel MctB; loss of these systems attenuates virulence. {{cite:CopperOverload}}{{cite:ZnCuReview}} Paradoxically, serum zinc is typically low in active TB — a redistribution of zinc from circulation into tissue driven by the same acute-phase cytokines, not dietary deficiency. {{cite:LowZnCu}}

Manganese completes the picture. Neutrophil calprotectin (S100A8/A9) sequesters Mn2+ and Zn2+ extracellularly, while NRAMP1/SLC11A1 pumps Fe2+ and Mn2+ out of the phagosome — and SLC11A1 polymorphisms are reproducibly associated with TB susceptibility. {{cite:Calprotectin}}{{cite:NRAMP1}}

MetalDirection in TBMeaning
Iron (serum)LowHepcidin-driven withholding; not deficiency
Iron (macrophage/tissue)Retained / loadedSeverity marker; loading worsens outcomes
FerritinHighStorage plus inflammation; tracks severity
Copper / Zinc (phagosome)High (host-imposed)Metal intoxication as a killing weapon
Zinc (serum)LowRedistribution to tissue; not deficiency
Manganese (phagosome)WithheldCalprotectin/NRAMP1 starvation

In sum, the TB metallome is defined by two opposing maneuvers at the host–pathogen interface: iron and manganese withholding on one side, copper and zinc intoxication on the other — a coordinated metallomic assault that Mtb has evolved an equally specific toolkit to survive.

sections.title: Nutritional Immunity
sections.html:
Nutritional Immunity

Nutritional immunity is the host's deliberate restriction of micronutrient metals to starve an invading pathogen, and in tuberculosis it operates as an integrated system of proteins rather than a set of isolated effectors. Read together, these proteins explain why the metallomic signature of active TB looks the way it does — and they dictate how that signature must be interpreted clinically.

The master switch is hepcidin. Driven by IL-6 during active infection, hepcidin binds and degrades ferroportin, shutting down iron export from enterocytes and macrophages; the result is hypoferremia, iron retention in the reticuloendothelial system, and the functional anemia of inflammation. {{cite:HepcidinAxis2}} Downstream, a layered defense limits the iron that does circulate. Transferrin and lactoferrin chelate free Fe3+, denying it to the bacillus; lactoferrin specifically contributes to antimycobacterial defense and reduces Mtb burden in iron-overloaded hosts. {{cite:Lactoferrin}} Lipocalin-2 (siderocalin / NGAL) adds a targeted countermeasure: rather than binding iron, it binds Mtb's iron-laden carboxymycobactin directly, intercepting the siderophore mid-piracy and exerting a bacteriostatic effect reversible by iron. {{cite:Siderocalin}} Calprotectin extends nutritional immunity beyond iron, sequestering manganese and zinc at the host–pathogen interface, {{cite:Calprotectin2}} while ferritin serves dual duty as intracellular iron storage and a circulating severity marker.

This system generates a single, decisive interpretive rule. In active TB, low serum iron and low serum zinc are usually the host deliberately starving M. tuberculosis — not nutritional deficiencies to correct. Hypoferremia is hepcidin-mediated sequestration; {{cite:HepcidinAxis2}} hypozincemia is cytokine-driven redistribution of zinc from blood into tissue. {{cite:LowZnCu2}} Both are host defense to be supported, not overridden. Anemia in TB is common and predicts worse outcomes, but it is largely anemia of inflammation; even studies documenting coexisting iron deficiency caution explicitly against universal iron therapy because excess iron may harm TB patients. {{cite:AnemiaMortality}}

The clinical corollaries follow directly. First, this is precisely why iron supplementation is a STOP in active TB (detailed in the Interventions section): exogenous iron can feed the very piracy machinery the host is working to defeat, and iron loading is independently associated with worse outcomes. {{cite:HostIronStatus2}} Second, because the host's strategy is sequestration, supporting that sequestration is the rational direction — for example, lactoferrin, which reinforces iron withholding rather than supplying free iron, and which lowers mycobacterial burden in iron-overloaded models. {{cite:Lactoferrin}} The interpretive frame is therefore inverted from ordinary nutrition: in active TB, a "low" metal is most often a measure of host defense in progress, and the therapeutic question is whether to reinforce it, never reflexively to reverse it.
